India will go into the opening Test against New Zealand at the Basin Reserve with four fast-bowling options, captain Shubman Gill confirmed on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), even as he admitted that choosing the right combination from a pool of six in-form pacers was proving to be a challenging exercise.
“Honestly, it is a bit of a headache, but a good kind of headache to have. All the fast bowlers stepped up in the ODI series. Gurnoor (Brar) did really well, Anshul (Kamboj) did really well. Even Harshit (Rana) and Siraj (Mohammed Siraj) in the last match that he played did pretty well,” Gill said during a press conference on Tuesday (November 17).
“We are still deciding on the final combination, which fast bowlers to go with, but you will definitely see four. We will be playing with four fast bowlers, that’s for sure.”
The decision, however, is unlikely to be straightforward. Gill indicated that India was looking at seven specialist batters, with the composition of the lower order depending on the bowling combination.
“Ideally, we are looking at seven proper batsmen and then the No. 8 and 9 would depend on the combination. Akash (Deep) can bat a bit, Anshul (Kamboj) can bat a bit and even if we go with (Nitish Kumar) Reddy, he is a proper batsman,” he said.
The nature of the Basin Reserve surface and the demands of bowling in Wellington’s notorious winds have added to the selection conundrum. Gill stressed that India would need different kinds of fast bowlers to cover the various phases of a five-day contest, particularly when the Kookaburra ball gets older and loses some of its movement.
“We have seen that at times on days three, four and five, the wicket, especially with the old ball, does go a little flat. From our fast-bowling unit, we would want someone who has pace and someone who can hit the areas consistently. And then, obviously, one spinner to control things from one end,” he said.
“Once the ball gets a bit old, the seam gets a bit weary. The ball doesn’t move as much off the pitch as it does with the new ball. You need someone who can hit the deck hard and create those chances again and again.”
He identified height and pace as important attributes, with the choice between the tall Gurnoor Brar and Prasidh Krishna likely to be dictated by who the team believes can offer more over the course of five days.
“Having at least a couple of bowlers who can hit the deck hard and bowl in the high 135s is important. Someone who is bowling fast, someone who is tall — between Gurnoor and Prasidh, whoever we think can give us more over the five days, is the one we will pick,” he said.
Gill was also candid about the challenges posed by the wind at the Basin Reserve, where bowlers operating against it could find their workload particularly demanding. While the team has attempted to prepare for the conditions with 13 of the 16, the captain acknowledged that there was only so much that could be replicated in practice.
“I believe it is much more difficult for the bowlers than it is for the batsmen. If someone is bowling 15-20 overs and has to bowl half of those against the wind, it is a pretty tough job,” he said.
“You can try to replicate it as much as you can in the nets, but there is only that much you can replicate. Only when you play and experience it do you get the real experience.”
Gill, meanwhile, dismissed suggestions that Rishabh Pant’s lack of match practice could be a concern for the team management. The wicketkeeper-batter has had limited competitive cricket since August, with just one innings in the Irani Trophy, but the captain believes his experience and ability to deliver in challenging overseas conditions outweigh those concerns.
“Not really. He is probably one of the most experienced and senior contenders in the team. I don’t know exactly how many matches he has played, but I think he has played around 50 Test matches, which is a lot,” Gill said.
Backing Pant’s credentials, Gill pointed to the batter’s remarkable record of scoring Test hundreds in challenging overseas conditions. Pant has registered centuries in Australia, England and South Africa, leaving New Zealand as the only one of those four major overseas destinations where he is yet to score a Test hundred.
“Given the kind of player and the quality that he brings, he has scored hundreds all over the world. As a wicketkeeper, he has scored hundreds in Australia, South Africa and England. It is probably the only country where he hasn’t, so I think he would also be looking forward to that,” Gill said.
Gill made no secret of the importance attached to the series, admitting that if given a choice among the three formats on this tour, the Test series would have been his preferred target.
“If someone had asked me a month ago which of these three series I would have liked to win, it would definitely have been the Test series. I am very happy that we were able to win the T20I and ODI series. Nothing like it if we are able to win the Test series as well. It will be a perfect tour,” he said.
However, Gill was quick to acknowledge the difficulty of achieving that against a New Zealand side that has traditionally been formidable at home. He also recalled India’s struggles during its previous visit, when the host exploited the visitors’ shortcomings, particularly with its use of the short ball.
The Indian captain who was a travelling reserve the last time it toured New Zealand in 2019-20 believes the lessons from that series have been factored into the team’s preparations and that the variety in its pace attack should help it counter different challenges.
“They challenged us in a lot of different areas. They knew exactly how to exploit our weaknesses and challenge us according to their strengths. We were probably not as prepared to counter those challenges,” he said.
“That’s also the reason for playing four fast bowlers. You want to cover all the aspects — if there is enough in the wicket, someone who can hit the areas consistently, and if the ball is not doing that, someone who can bend their back and bowl the hard length for a consistent period.”
Having insisted on extended preparation windows ahead of important assignments, Gill was pleased that India had managed to get adequate time in New Zealand, including a substantial block of training before the Test series.
“As a side, we don’t want to feel that we left any stones unturned. We want to feel that we have prepared for everything and have all the answers. Now it is all about execution,” he said.
